The material investigated was a new high gamma-prime content polycrystalline nickel-based superalloy, referred to as Alloy 11.
The average sizes of the gamma-prime precipitate populations were: primary - 430 nm, secondary - 76 nm, and tertiary - 25 nm.
At temperatures below 500°C, no apparent changes in the elemental distributions were observed during in-situ heating.
At 800°C, the tertiary gamma-prime precipitates began to dissolve, while the primary and secondary gamma-prime remained stable.
By 900°C, the secondary gamma-prime precipitates located near the grain boundaries had dissolved, and the tertiary gamma-prime population was completely dissolved.
The large primary gamma-prime particle at the top right corner remained undissolved even at 950°C, while the fine secondary and tertiary gamma-prime populations had disappeared.

The Gibbs-Thomson effect, which relates the interfacial concentration to the particle curvature, was used to explain the earlier dissolution of the smaller tertiary gamma-prime precipitates compared to the larger secondary gamma-prime.
The supersaturation parameter, k, was higher for the tertiary gamma-prime precipitates compared to the secondary gamma-prime, leading to faster dissolution kinetics for the smaller particles.
The in-situ STEM-EELS technique provided spatially resolved information on the elemental distributions and compositional changes during the heating of the thin TEM lamella samples.

The model-based quantification of the EELS measurements allowed for the tracking of relative differences in elemental concentrations, although the absolute values should be treated as rough estimations.
